questions.q: What does the Security Debugger actually show once it's switched on?
options: A list of all users currently logged into the instance
A list of every scheduled job currently running
Every ACL evaluated for the page load, with a pass/fail reason for each
The full change history of every record on the table
questions.explain: The Security Debugger (Debug Security Rules) produces a security log naming every ACL evaluated and why each one passed or failed.

questions.q: What advantage does the Security Debugger have over manually filtering the Access Control list?
options: It disables all ACLs temporarily so the user can access the record
It only works for field-level ACLs, not table-level ones
It edits the failing ACL automatically
It hands you the real evaluation trace for the exact page, instead of requiring you to reason through every ACL that might apply
questions.explain: Instead of guessing which ACLs apply, the debugger reproduces the actual evaluation for that page load, naming the exact ACLs and outcomes.

questions.q: What is required to edit an ACL record, and how is it activated?
options: The itil role, activated automatically on login
No special role is needed since all admins can always edit ACLs
The catalog_admin role, activated through System Properties
The security_admin role, activated through Elevate Roles in the profile menu
questions.explain: Editing sys_security_acl records requires the security_admin role, which is turned on deliberately via Elevate Roles, not held permanently active.

questions.q: Why is security_admin deliberately NOT always-on, even for a full admin?
options: Because it's powerful enough to bypass ACL script evaluation, so leaving it always active risks an admin accidentally breaking the ACL that governs ACL editing itself, with no safety net
It conflicts with the itil role if both are active simultaneously
ServiceNow licensing restricts how many users can hold it at once
It would slow down page load times too much
questions.explain: Requiring deliberate elevation means the bypass power is only active for the specific session where it's intended, preserving normal ACL enforcement the rest of the time.

questions.q: In the repeatable troubleshooting order given in this lesson, when should an admin actually elevate roles?
options: Only when they need to edit the ACL record itself to fix it, not merely to read or troubleshoot it
Never — elevation should be avoided even when fixing a broken ACL
Only after restarting the instance
At the very start of every troubleshooting session, before looking at anything
questions.explain: Reading and troubleshooting ACLs rarely requires security_admin; it's needed specifically when the fix means editing the ACL record.
